n0001.title: What If We Had Bigger Brains?
n0001.gist: Drawing on computational theory, neuroscience, and AI, the author argues that bigger brains would not simply think more but would navigate deeper networks of computational reducibility, reshaping language, abstraction, and society in ways only partly comprehensible to minds like ours.
n0001.sourceHeading: What If We Had Bigger Brains? Imagining Minds beyond Ours

n0002.title: Cats Don't Talk
n0002.gist: Human-scale brains manage to navigate an irreducibly complex world only by exploiting pockets of computational reducibility, and it is this capacity—reflected in concepts, words, and language—that a bigger brain could extend well beyond our current 30,000-word vocabulary.

n0003.title: Cats Don't Talk
n0003.gist: Neural networks have crossed a series of capability thresholds as they scale, raising the question of what qualitatively new abilities might emerge in brains far larger than our own.

n0013.title: Pockets of Reducibility
n0013.gist: Although brains cannot escape the world's underlying computational irreducibility, they succeed by exploiting the infinite pockets of computational reducibility embedded within it.

n0014.navLabel: Computational Equivalence implies generic systems reach maximal sophistication beyond a low threshold

n0015.navLabel: Brains specifically compute by turning large sensory input into decisions about what to do next

n0016.navLabel: The world is full of computational irreducibility, where outcomes require step-by-step simulation

n0018.navLabel: Brains exploit pockets of computational reducibility to jump ahead without simulating every detail

n0019.navLabel: Progress of science identifies more pockets of reducibility; bigger brains might hold more of them in mind

n0020.title: Concepts and Abstraction
n0020.gist: Concepts and words compress the world's complexity into a manageable, roughly 30,000-item vocabulary, and abstraction lets us generalize across many specific pockets of reducibility into higher-level categories.

n0021.navLabel: Brains compress world complexity into concepts and language, like symbolizing many images as 'rock'

n0022.navLabel: Human languages converge on ~30,000 words, raising whether bigger brains could handle millions more

n0023.navLabel: Our 30,000 words suffice only because we chose which features of the world to name

n0024.navLabel: Computational irreducibility guarantees we'll eventually meet things our current concepts can't describe

n0025.navLabel: Abstraction groups specifics like 'tiger' and 'lion' into general categories like 'big cats' to prevent endless concept growth

n0026.navLabel: Concepts as pockets of reducibility form networks, and abstraction reflects these networks, which can recurse

n0027.title: Emergent Concepts and Communication
n0027.gist: Neural networks spontaneously discover millions of emergent concepts, but a concept only becomes a genuinely useful abstraction when it can be packaged into language and reliably transferred between minds.

n0028.navLabel: Neural nets spontaneously form millions of emergent concepts as clusters in feature space, mostly unnamed by us

n0029.navLabel: Whether emergent concepts are useful abstractions depends on usefulness independent of their originating layer

n0030.navLabel: Language's core role is transferring thoughts between minds by packaging activity into transportable concepts

n0031.navLabel: Translation between minds is imprecise, but saying more generally yields more faithful translation

n0032.title: Bigger Brains and Language
n0032.gist: A bigger brain, harboring more emergent concepts, would need richer language to communicate them precisely, potentially producing minds whose computations look less comprehensible yet still remain describable through abstraction.

n0033.navLabel: Bigger brains with more emergent concepts would need more words or richer compositional language, unlike dogs' isolated words

n0034.navLabel: Language models the world via finite primitives whose network of reducibility pockets can never be complete

n0035.navLabel: A bigger brain's computation might look more irreducible yet remain describable through brain-like abstraction

n0036.navLabel: Computation's universality makes discussing bigger-than-human minds more plausible than a cat understanding algebra

n0037.title: How Brains Seem to Work
n0037.gist: Brains across species and even artificial neural networks share a common architecture—many sensory inputs collapsed through layered processing into a single stream of decisions—whose core capabilities depend on scale, working memory, and generalization rather than fine biological detail.

n0038.title: Brain Anatomy and Evolution
n0038.gist: Across animals and even large language models, brains share a basic architecture of massive sensory input funneled through layered neurons into a single decisive output, a structure likely rooted in the evolutionary need to choose one direction of movement at a time.

n0040.navLabel: Brains turn large sensory input into small numbers of action decisions, but how remains to be explained

n0041.navLabel: Human brains funnel millions of sensors through ~100 billion neurons into a majority-vote decision structure

n0042.navLabel: Brain architecture scales with sensor number and folds to reduce connection length across animals

n0043.navLabel: Brains likely arose so animals could choose one direction of movement, yielding a single stream of decisions and consciousness

n0044.navLabel: LLMs mirror brain operation but separate training from thinking, unlike brains' interspersed learning

n0045.navLabel: Core brain-like capabilities depend on many inputs, few outputs, irreducible computation, and relative size, not biological detail

n0046.title: Memory and Generalization
n0046.gist: What matters most for brain-like systems is not memorizing training data but generalizing appropriately within the bounds of limited working memory and unconscious processing, always constrained to the pockets of computational reducibility they can access.

n0047.navLabel: Memory in neural nets and brains is encoded in connection weights, with capacity scaling with weight count

n0048.navLabel: What matters is generalizing appropriately to new inputs, not memorizing training specifics

n0049.navLabel: Simple neural net architectures generalize in ways aligned with human brains due to shared brain-like universality

n0050.navLabel: Both brains and neural nets have fixed neuron counts and only limited recycling of output to input

n0051.navLabel: Working memory limits, roughly 5-7 chunks in adults, constrain brain-like computation and scale with brain development

n0052.navLabel: Conscious thought is a thin thread derived from a vast ocean of unconscious neural activity

n0053.navLabel: Neural nets show generic learning ability across input types, and brains likely share this genericity

n0054.navLabel: How bigger brains might access further pockets of reducibility beyond current ones is the core question

n0055.title: Language and Beyond
n0055.gist: Language packages the discrete concepts brains extract from continuous neural activity into a robust, sequential, compositional system, but bigger brains might support richer grammars, multiway threads of thought, or entirely different modalities like direct image communication.

n0056.title: Concepts as Language
n0056.gist: Brains compress the world's complexity into discrete, robust concepts, and only by packaging these into language-like symbols can a single brain reliably preserve and communicate thoughts over time.

n0058.navLabel: Brains compress world complexity by equivalencing many inputs into one representation, ignoring pixel-level detail

n0059.navLabel: An equivalence class corresponds to a neural attractor that we describe at a higher level as a 'concept'

n0060.navLabel: Conscious experience extracts discrete concepts as higher-level units from mostly irreducible neural activity

n0061.navLabel: Robust constructs seem discrete because no computational paradigm supports continuous concept spaces

n0062.navLabel: Packaging neural activity into concepts, i.e. language, enables both communication and single-brain memory

n0063.navLabel: Preserving a thought across a continually changing neural environment requires packaging it into robust language-like elements

n0064.navLabel: Human language nests phrases context-freely, parseable recursively up to working memory's stack limits

n0065.title: Bigger Brains, Richer Grammar
n0065.gist: Bigger brains could plausibly manage more concepts and deeper nested grammar thanks to larger working memory, but pushing language into genuinely non-context-free structures would require irreducible computation incompatible with brain-like operation.

n0066.navLabel: Ordinary language is presented sequentially, connected to the brain's single thread of conscious experience

n0067.navLabel: Despite surface diversity, human languages share fundamental parts of speech and structural concepts

n0068.navLabel: Whether language commonalities stem from shared history, sensory experience, or brain construction remains unclear

n0072.navLabel: Non-context-free language requiring arbitrary computation falls outside brain-like single-thread decision workflows

n0074.title: Beyond Sequential Language
n0074.gist: Beyond ordinary sequential language, one can imagine multiway minds with branching threads of thought or brains equipped to communicate directly in images, though such possibilities depend on having fundamentally different cognitive hardware, not just more neurons.

n0075.navLabel: Multiway systems with branching threads would require different architecture, not just more neurons

n0076.navLabel: Language communicated as sequences, though math and diagrams use 2D or graph structures

n0077.navLabel: Communicating mental images directly might require reducing them to discrete concepts and language anyway

n0081.title: Sensors and Actuators
n0081.gist: The features and concepts a brain finds useful depend jointly on the kind of sensory data it receives and the actions it can take, so bigger brains would handle more features and actuators, but different senses or timescales could yield entirely different, equally valid conceptual worlds.

n0082.title: Sensory Features and Concepts
n0082.gist: Brains distill raw sensory data into a limited set of learned features tied to whatever pockets of computational reducibility are useful, leaving most of the space of possible images or data in an unfamiliar 'interconcept space' that a bigger brain could better navigate.

n0084.navLabel: Human brains distill correlated raw sensor data into a few more independent features quickly

n0085.navLabel: Features correspond to pockets of computational reducibility learned as useful for deriving decisions

n0086.navLabel: What counts as useful features depends on whether experience is indigenous or technology-mediated

n0087.navLabel: Programs can generate images so unfamiliar that we cannot tell what's going on in them

n0089.navLabel: Unrecognized image pieces reflect interconcept space, pockets of reducibility we aren't familiar with

n0091.navLabel: Bigger brains could track more features and concepts, though irreducibility ultimately overpowers them

n0092.title: Actuators and Technology
n0092.gist: While brains our size suffice for indigenous human experience, technology can overload them, and controlling unfamiliar actuators—like quadcopters with many degrees of freedom—may require brains bigger than ours.

n0093.navLabel: Brains our size suffice for indigenous experience but technology can overload them

n0094.navLabel: Different brains using different primitive concepts should still be translatable if sampling similar environments

n0095.navLabel: Brains sampling different slices of reality via technology may need entirely different useful features

n0096.navLabel: Usefulness of features depends on what actions and capabilities, pure or technologically augmented, allow

n0097.navLabel: Technology gives us actuators beyond muscles that brains like ours may fail to operate

n0098.navLabel: Humans couldn't control quadcopters unaided, suggesting bigger brains might handle more degrees of freedom

n0099.title: Different Senses, Different Concepts
n0099.gist: Different sensory modalities, distributed sensor arrays, or altered timescales would each expose different pockets of computational reducibility, meaning that a differently-sensed world might need a differently-sized brain rather than simply a bigger one.

n0100.navLabel: Controlling actuators involves both addressing degrees of freedom and finding pockets of reducibility to jump ahead

n0101.navLabel: Indigenous experience relies on reducibility from familiar natural laws like motion of objects

n0102.navLabel: A smell-based brain like a dog's would build concepts from odor space rather than geometry

n0103.navLabel: Smell-based animals may succeed with smaller brains than sight-based animals need

n0104.navLabel: Distributed sensor arrays like IoT devices would likely require a bigger brain to track

n0105.navLabel: Faster timescales of sensory input might reveal quantum optics effects beyond ordinary perception

n0106.title: Abstraction
n0106.gist: Abstraction—the historical process of building towers of concepts atop concepts—is itself a network of pockets of computational reducibility, one that bigger brains could navigate further, though ultimately even expanding brains cannot outrun the irreducible growth of knowledge and its rare but inevitable grand analogies.

n0107.title: Origins of Abstraction
n0107.gist: Human abstraction developed slowly, beginning with language and concepts remote from direct experience, and accelerated through logic, mathematics, algebra, and eventually 19th-century formal symbolic systems.

n0109.navLabel: Bigger brains might make abstraction easier or reach fundamentally higher levels of it

n0110.navLabel: Basic perception already involves abstraction, but asking 'what if?' marks a further level

n0111.navLabel: Language's invention marked the greatest early leap in abstraction, seen in numbers, money, future

n0112.navLabel: Abstraction develops by packaging observed similarities into concepts, then building towers upon them

n0113.navLabel: Abstraction moved slowly through theology, syllogistic logic, and mathematics before reaching pure numbers

n0114.navLabel: Algebra advanced abstraction, but 19th-century formal symbolic systems accelerated it further

n0115.title: Towers of Abstraction
n0115.gist: Abstraction lets us reason about whole classes of things via pockets of computational reducibility, but the resulting towers rest on scaffolding of analogy and remain shadowed by underlying computational irreducibility, which a bigger brain could push further into, without ever eliminating.

n0116.navLabel: Modern computation emerged from this tradition, with mathematics building towers from numbers to category theory

n0117.navLabel: Abstraction lets us think about classes of things, but often grows remote from raw perception

n0118.navLabel: How high a concept sits on the abstraction tower shows in how much must be explained to reach it

n0119.navLabel: Highly abstract thinking works through analogies to more familiar things, imperfect scaffolding notwithstanding

n0120.navLabel: Abstraction reflects pockets of computational reducibility organized into networks that can be hard to navigate

n0121.navLabel: Brains rely on abstraction because, unlike computers, they can't go through all the steps

n0122.navLabel: A bigger brain could reach further into the network of abstraction without escaping irreducibility

n0123.title: Abstraction and the Ruliad
n0123.gist: The ruliad—the entangled limit of all computation and abstraction—reveals that our perceived laws of physics arise specifically from brains being computationally bounded with a single persistent thread of experience, features that would likely persist even in bigger, still brain-like minds.

n0124.navLabel: Discovering computational irreducibility in the computational universe felt like a structural shock to intuition

n0125.navLabel: Metamathematics suggests nested levels of abstraction culminating in the ruliad encompassing them all

n0126.navLabel: The ruliad is the entangled limit of all computation and all possible abstractions

n0127.navLabel: Brains parse the irreducible ruliad in a way that yields our perceived core laws of physics

n0128.navLabel: Bigger brains of the same kind would still perceive the same physics if computationally bounded with one thread

n0129.navLabel: Understanding physics further requires understanding more about what we're like as observers

n0130.navLabel: Bigger brains would still pale against ruliad irreducibility, though each new reducibility pocket yields new law

n0131.title: Knowledge, Analogies and Limits
n0131.gist: As knowledge grows irreducibly and diverges across specialties, only bigger brains or AIs could hope to draw the rare 'grand analogies' that connect distant domains, though the ruliad's underlying homogeneity guarantees such connections are always latent, if not always practically discoverable.

n0132.navLabel: New abstractions open new goals for thinking and making, far from indigenous human goals

n0133.navLabel: An infinite network of abstraction towers exists, with bigger brains or AIs able to pursue many different paths

n0134.navLabel: Reaching higher abstraction mixes education's role with brains' intrinsic computational ability

n0135.navLabel: Growing civilizational knowledge has outpaced what a brain our size can commit to memory

n0136.navLabel: Grand analogies across siloed knowledge domains are where bigger brains or AIs go beyond us

n0137.navLabel: The ruliad's homogeneity guarantees grand analogies exist, even if only at an atomic, formal level

n0138.navLabel: Irreducibility guarantees new knowledge and surprises, even if some knowledge seems too abstruse to matter

n0139.title: Computational Language
n0139.gist: Computational language, exemplified by the Wolfram Language, shows what lies beyond ordinary human language—higher-order functions and symbolic uniformity that let one 'go meta'—but pushing further into pure structures like combinators or graph-based expressions quickly exceeds what any brain-like system can process.

n0140.title: Beyond Ordinary Language
n0140.gist: Formally, compositional language could encode any computation, but this is impractical; the real clue to what lies beyond ordinary language is computational language, which brains use not to run programs but to represent thoughts.

n0142.navLabel: Compositional language might not be the top; bigger brains might reach something beyond it

n0143.navLabel: Compositional language formally encodes universal computation, but not in any practically useful sense

n0144.navLabel: Computational language, not ordinary language, offers the clue to what lies beyond human language

n0145.navLabel: Computational language differs for computers and brains, with computers mainly evaluating expressions

n0146.navLabel: Brains use Wolfram Language expressions as representations of thought, not as programs to run

n0147.navLabel: Computational language represents thoughts about numbers, real-world entities, and higher-level abstract structures

n0148.title: Higher-Order Functions
n0148.gist: Computational language's higher-order functions, like NestList, let one operate on functions themselves rather than mere data—a 'meta' capability rare in human language but made natural by representing everything uniformly as symbolic expressions.

n0154.navLabel: Higher-order operations become possible because everything is represented uniformly as a symbolic expression

n0155.navLabel: Uniform representation enables higher-order manipulation, though names are anchored to ordinary English words

n0156.title: Combinators and Abstraction Limits
n0156.gist: Purely structural constructs like combinators are almost impossible for humans to grasp because they lack anchoring to familiar concepts, and mastering any new higher-order abstraction seems to require gradually feeling out its pocket of reducibility one level at a time—a process a bigger brain might accelerate, but perhaps not for combinators, which may lie beyond any brain-like system.

n0157.navLabel: Combinators show that operations like addition can be represented purely structurally, without anchoring

n0159.navLabel: Combinators remain nearly impenetrable because they lack anchoring to concepts brains already grasp

n0160.navLabel: Grokking higher-order constructs takes months or years, progressing one level at a time

n0161.navLabel: Learning a new construct means feeling out irreducibility until finding its pocket of reducibility

n0162.navLabel: A bigger brain might speed this feeling-out, but combinators may lie beyond any brain-like system per the Principle of Computational Equivalence

n0163.title: Symbolic Expressions and Brain Limits
n0163.gist: Symbolic expressions succeed as a bridge between human thought and computation because their tree-like grammar matches how brains process language, but once structures become graphs or hypergraphs requiring multiple simultaneous threads of thought, they exceed what any single brain-like system can handle.

n0165.navLabel: Higher-order functions may relate to category theory's morphisms, which assume computational reducibility

n0166.navLabel: Computational language design's core art is casting abstruse structural ideas into accessible, human-friendly form

n0167.navLabel: Bridging foundations to familiarity is achievable through education, not requiring a bigger brain, as functional programming shows

n0168.navLabel: Wolfram Language's symbolic expressions are set up to match how brains actually work

n0169.navLabel: Symbolic expressions' tree-like grammar mirrors human language grammar, letting limited working memory cope with computational language

n0170.navLabel: Graph- or hypergraph-structured symbolic expressions require multiple threads of thought that brain-like systems can't manage

n0171.title: Many Brains Together
n0171.gist: Because individual brains maintain only a single thread of experience, coordinated multi-threaded 'thinking' is achieved instead through standardized communication among many brains, and bigger brains might support far more complex social structures than the graphs that describe human society today.
n0171.sourceHeading: Many Brains Together: The Formation of Society

n0172.title: From One Mind to Many
n0172.gist: Evolution gave individual brains just one thread of experience, so coordinated group behavior in societies must instead arise from communication between many separate single-threaded brains.

n0176.navLabel: Just as neuron firings collapse to one conclusion in a brain, many brains' conclusions must be collected into coordinated outcomes

n0177.navLabel: Robust coordination requires standardized communication like language rather than unreliable direct 'telepathic' sharing of neuron firings

n0178.title: Language and Social Coordination
n0178.gist: Standardized communication both requires and sustains social coordination, and while human societies rely on maintaining something like a single 'thread of society', bigger brains might manage far more complex, hypergraph-like social structures.

n0184.title: Minds beyond Ours
n0184.gist: Bigger, brain-like minds—biological or artificial—would occupy larger regions of the computational 'ruliad' by commanding more concepts and higher-order abstractions, yet would remain only partly comprehensible to us, just as a mind spanning the entire ruliad would cease to have any coherent, individual thread of experience at all.

n0185.gist: Rather than removing the defining limitations of brain-like computation, this exploration conservatively imagines brains simply scaled up in neurons and connections, following capability thresholds already glimpsed in animals and artificial neural networks.

n0188.navLabel: Removing brain-like limitations yields more computation but not something recognizable as 'a mind like ours'

n0192.navLabel: Maintaining the same architecture keeps a single thread of experience, but allows more raw concepts or nested qualifiers

n0193.title: Going Meta and Abstraction
n0193.gist: The most qualitatively distinct capability bigger brains might gain is routinely 'going meta'—operating with higher-order abstractions—though where such abstraction leads remains as much a matter of historical accident as of raw brain capacity.

n0201.title: Minds in Rulial Space
n0201.gist: Interacting with a bigger brain would be like a dog overhearing philosophy—we'd grasp only simplified fragments—because such minds, biological or artificial, occupy larger regions of the ruliad than ours, with a mind spanning the whole ruliad ultimately dissolving into no coherent mind at all.
